title: Road
content: A road is a route intended or used for vehicular or other traffic. A driver must understand that a road environment includes the carriageway, lanes, shoulders, junctions, crossings, signs, markings, pedestrians, cyclists, roadside objects, and changing hazards.

title: Left-hand traffic
content: Zimbabwe drives on the left-hand side of the road. This affects normal lane positioning, the side used for overtaking, roundabout circulation, turning behaviour, and the interpretation of traffic approaching from different directions.

title: Priority versus permission
content: Priority means which road user is entitled or expected to proceed before another under the applicable rule. Permission means that a movement is not prohibited, but it is still only safe when conditions allow it. A driver must never interpret 'I have priority' as 'I may drive regardless of danger.'

title: Purpose of road signs
content: Road signs communicate control, warning, guidance, information, restrictions, or instructions to road users. A strong learner should identify sign type, shape, colour scheme, symbol or wording, whether the sign warns, commands, prohibits, guides, or informs, and what action should follow.

title: Regulatory signs
content: Regulatory signs impose or communicate traffic controls and restrictions. Examples include stop, give way, speed restriction, no entry, no overtaking, no U-turn, no parking, no stopping, prohibited turns, compulsory movements. Regulatory = 'this is the rule you must obey.'

title: Warning signs
content: Warning signs alert drivers to hazards, road conditions or unusual circumstances ahead. Typical subjects: bends, junctions, pedestrian activity, children or schools, animals, road narrowing, steep gradients, slippery surfaces, railway crossings, traffic signals. Warning = 'pay attention to what is ahead and prepare.'

title: Mandatory signs
content: Mandatory signs tell road users that a particular action or direction is required. Examples: proceed in a specified direction, keep to a specified side, use a particular route, compulsory turning or movement. 'Mandatory tells you what you must do. Prohibitory tells you what you must not do.'

title: Prohibitory signs
content: Prohibitory signs prohibit a movement, action, vehicle category, or use. Common examples: no entry, no overtaking, no U-turn, no right turn, speed restriction, no parking, no stopping. Learners often confuse 'no parking' with 'no stopping' — teach them as different restrictions.

title: Stop sign
content: A stop sign requires a driver to stop at the appropriate stop line or stopping point and comply with the applicable give-way rule before proceeding. Stopping is an action, not merely slowing down. A rolling stop is not the same thing as a complete stop.

title: Give-way sign
content: A give-way sign tells the approaching driver that priority belongs to traffic with precedence under the applicable junction arrangement. The driver should approach in a manner that allows the vehicle to stop and should yield when required.

title: Speed restriction sign
content: A speed restriction sign establishes a maximum permitted speed for the controlled road section. A maximum speed is not a target speed. The safe speed can be lower because of rain, pedestrians, congestion, poor visibility, road surface, animals, vehicle condition, load, bends, hills, temporary hazards.

title: Sign plates and supplementary information
content: A supplementary plate can qualify the main sign by giving distance, direction, time, vehicle class, exception, length of restriction, conditions. Teach learners to read the complete sign combination, not only the main symbol.

title: Centre lines
content: Centre lines separate opposing traffic streams. Their appearance, continuity and colour communicate different rules under the applicable sign and marking system. A driver should never cross a line simply because the road appears empty.

title: Continuous and double continuous lines
content: Continuous lines indicate stronger restriction on crossing than broken lines. Double continuous markings communicate a strong restriction and must be interpreted according to the applicable road-marking rule. Do not teach that every solid line means the same thing in every location.

title: Lane arrows
content: Lane arrows tell drivers where traffic in a lane is intended or required to proceed. A driver should choose the correct lane early, signal where appropriate, follow the arrow, avoid last-second cutting across lanes. Lane arrows are especially important before signalised junctions, roundabouts, lane splits, turn-only lanes.

title: Stop line
content: A stop line identifies where a vehicle should stop when required by the associated control. At a traffic signal or stop sign, stopping after the line can place the vehicle in the conflict area and obstruct pedestrians or cross traffic.

title: Pedestrian crossing markings
content: Crossing markings indicate an area used by pedestrians to cross the carriageway. Drivers should reduce speed when approaching, observe pedestrians, stop when required, avoid overtaking or positioning that hides pedestrians.

title: Traffic light basics
content: Traffic signals allocate movement through a controlled conflict point. General meaning: red = stop, green = movement permitted when the route is clear and no other restriction prevents proceeding, amber = transition toward stopping. The AI should never teach green as 'you can drive no matter what.'

title: Amber light reasoning
content: Amber is not a signal to accelerate through the junction. The driver should normally prepare to stop and stop where required if this can be done safely. 'Never create a greater hazard simply to beat a light.'

title: Arrows and lane-control signals
content: Directional arrows can control particular movements separately from the main signal. A driver must read the active signal, arrow direction, lane markings, turn prohibition, pedestrian movement.

title: Police or traffic officer control
content: A person lawfully directing traffic may give instructions that drivers must follow according to the applicable law. When a police officer or authorised traffic controller is physically controlling movement, the driver must not ignore that direction simply because a signal shows something different.

title: Priority hierarchy
content: At a junction, the driver should first identify the controls that determine movement: 1) authorised traffic control, 2) traffic signals, 3) regulatory signs and markings, 4) road layout and applicable right-of-way rules, 5) safe driving judgement.

title: Right of way
content: Right of way answers the question: 'Who should proceed first under the applicable rule?' The driver must assess signs, lines, lights, road shape, lane direction, pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles already committed to the junction.

title: Uncontrolled junctions
content: At an uncontrolled junction, no traffic light or explicit priority sign controls the conflict. A commonly taught Zimbabwe convention is that traffic approaching from the right is given precedence at an uncontrolled intersection. This should be treated as a Zimbabwe road-rule teaching point.

title: Roundabouts
content: At a roundabout, drivers must understand approach lane selection, direction of circulation, traffic already circulating, signals, lane arrows, exit selection, position before exiting, blind spots. A simple 'give way to the right' slogan is insufficient.

title: Merging
content: Merging is the process of joining another traffic stream. A safe merge requires speed matching, adequate gap, mirror checks, blind-spot checks, signal, smooth movement, no forcing of another road user.

title: Maximum speed versus safe speed
content: A posted maximum speed is a legal ceiling, not an instruction to drive at that speed in all conditions. Safe speed depends on visibility, surface, road geometry, traffic, pedestrians, weather, vehicle/load, expected hazards.

title: Speed on bends
content: Braking heavily during a bend can upset vehicle balance. Better roadcraft: reduce speed before the bend, select the appropriate gear, enter with a usable safety margin, maintain smooth steering, accelerate progressively when the road opens.

title: Speed downhill
content: Descending steep roads can cause speed to build quickly. Use appropriate gear, controlled braking, safe speed, increased following distance. Avoid relying continuously on the foot brake on a long descent because braking components can overheat.

title: Overtaking checklist
content: Before overtaking, ask: 1) Is overtaking legal here? 2) Is there sufficient visibility? 3) Is the road clear far enough ahead? 4) Is there enough acceleration/performance? 5) Is the gap still available? 6) Have mirrors and blind spots been checked? 7) Has the intention been signalled? 8) Can I return to my lane without forcing another vehicle to brake? If any answer is no, wait.

title: Places where overtaking is dangerous
content: Avoid overtaking where the road environment prevents adequate visibility or recovery space, including blind bends, crests, narrow bridges, restricted junction approaches, pedestrian conflict areas, railway crossings, areas with solid restriction markings, any location prohibited by sign or law.

title: Stopping versus parking
content: Stopping is a temporary halt. Parking generally means leaving a vehicle stationary for a longer period or for a purpose covered by the applicable parking rule. The legal distinction can depend on the regulation and sign.

title: Unsafe parking locations
content: Do not park where doing so blocks traffic, obstructs visibility, blocks a crossing, blocks a driveway or entrance, creates danger at a junction, hides a sign, obstructs emergency access, violates a local sign or restriction.

title: Vulnerable road users
content: Vulnerable road users have less physical protection. These include pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, children, elderly people, people with disabilities, roadside workers. Drivers must anticipate their presence and leave appropriate space.

title: Pedestrian crossings
content: Approach crossings at a speed that allows safe response. Watch for pedestrians waiting, pedestrians already crossing, children, cyclists, vehicles stopped near the crossing. Never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crossing.

title: Cyclists
content: When passing cyclists: allow generous lateral clearance, avoid passing at unsafe speed, check for oncoming traffic, expect wobbling or sudden movement, do not squeeze them toward kerbs or obstacles.

title: Tyres
content: Tyres are the only normal contact between vehicle and road. Inspect inflation, tread, visible damage, uneven wear, bulges, cuts. Underinflation can affect handling, braking and fuel consumption. Worn or damaged tyres reduce grip.

title: Brakes
content: A healthy braking system should give predictable stopping performance. Warning signs: soft/spongy pedal, unusual noise, pulling, vibration, warning light, increased stopping distance. The correct instructional response is to have the fault checked.

title: Lights
content: Lights serve two functions: help the driver see, and help others see the vehicle. Know the purpose of headlamps, dipped/low beam, main/high beam, brake lights, indicators, hazard warning lights, fog lamps, rear lights, number-plate illumination.

title: Rain
content: Rain can reduce visibility, increase stopping distance, reduce tyre grip, obscure road markings, create standing water. Response: slow down, increase following distance, use appropriate lights, use wipers, avoid abrupt control inputs.

title: Aquaplaning
content: Aquaplaning/hydroplaning occurs when water reduces tyre contact with the road. Risk increases with standing water, higher speed, worn tyres. If it occurs: remain calm, avoid abrupt braking, ease off the accelerator, hold a steady course, allow the tyres to regain contact.

title: Night driving
content: Night driving reduces detection time and changes how hazards are perceived. Good practice: reduce speed as visibility falls, keep windscreen and lights clean, use high beam only where appropriate and without dazzling others, dip lights when required, expect pedestrians, cyclists and animals to be harder to see.

title: Skid causes
content: Skids occur when available tyre grip is exceeded. Causes can include excessive speed, sudden steering, harsh braking, acceleration on low-grip surfaces, poor tyres, water, loose gravel, oil or mud.

title: Responding to a skid
content: The correct recovery action depends on whether the vehicle is understeering, oversteering, braking-locking, or otherwise losing grip. General principle: stay calm, avoid panic inputs, look where you want to travel, make smooth control inputs, regain tyre grip.

title: First priority after a crash
content: After an accident: 1) protect life, 2) prevent further collision where possible, 3) call appropriate emergency services, 4) assist injured people within your training, 5) exchange/report required information under the applicable law. Do not create another collision while trying to help.

title: Alcohol
content: Alcohol impairs judgement, reaction, attention, coordination, risk assessment. The safest driving principle is not to drive after drinking. For legal threshold questions, use the current Zimbabwe law.

title: Fatigue
content: Fatigue reduces attention, reaction time, decision quality, lane control. Warning signs: yawning, heavy eyelids, wandering lane position, missing signs, poor memory of recent kilometres. Correct response: stop safely and rest.

title: Learner licence age
content: Zimbabwe's 2023 Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations provide that a person under 16 may not be issued a learner's licence. The full licensing framework contains different requirements for different vehicle classes.

title: VID role
content: The Vehicle Inspectorate Department is responsible for functions that include vehicle inspection and testing for learner's licences and Certificates of Competency.
